etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English out, oute, from a combination of Old English ūt (“out”, preposition & adverb), from Proto-West Germanic *ūt, from Proto-Germanic *ūt (“out”); and Old English ūte (“outside; without”, adverb), from Proto-Germanic *ūtai (“out; outside”); both from Proto-Indo-European *úd (“upwards, away”).

Cognate with Scots oot, out (“out”), Saterland Frisian uut, uute (“out”), West Frisian út (“out”), Dutch uit (“out”), German Low German ut (“out”), German aus (“out”), Norwegian/Swedish ut, ute (“out; outside”), Danish ud, ude (“out; outside”).

definitions.definition: Away from the inside or centre.
Specifically, away from home or one's usual place.
Away from the doer, especially vigorously.
Away from, or at a distance from, some point of reference or focus.
(informal) Away, or at a distance, in time (relative to, and usually after, the present or a stated event) (often preceded by a stated time period and followed by "from")
Outside; not indoors.
(sports) Of the ball or other playing implement, so as to pass or be situated beyond the bounds of the playing area.
Into a state of non-operation or non-existence.
Shows that an activity has been completed to the point of exhaustion.
To the end; completely; so that nothing remains.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Psalm 4:23:
quote.text: Deceitful men shall not live out half their days.

quote.citation: 1984, "All cried out", song by English singer-songwriter Alison Moyet:
quote.text: I'm all cried out / You took a whole lot of loving for a handful of nothing

definitions.definition: Used to intensify or emphasize.
(of the sun, moon, stars, etc.) So as to be visible in the sky, and not covered by clouds, fog, etc.
Into a state of existence or visibility.
(cricket, baseball) Of a player, so as to be disqualified from playing further by some action of a member of the opposing team (such as being stumped in cricket).

quote.citation: 1876, The School newspaper Vol. [2 issues of vols. 31 and 32]., page 66:
quote.text: First ball hit me on the 'and, second 'ad me on the knee, the third was in my eye, the fourth bowled me out.

quote.citation: 1984, Official Baseball Guide, page 211:
quote.text: Hayes batted for Reed and grounded out, Murray unassisted.

quote.citation: 2007, Philip R. Craig, William G. Tapply, Third Strike: A Brady Coyne/J. W. Jackson Mystery, page 27:
quote.text: So, first guy, Larry strikes him out, good fastball in on his hands.

quote.citation: 2010, Mark Butcher, Paul Abraham, Learn to Play Cricket: Teach Yourself, page A-65:
quote.text: The striking batter is bowled out when the wicket is broken with the bowler's delivery. A batter is bowled out whether or not the ball is touched or deflected into the stumps by the batter.

definitions.definition: (informal, sometimes proscribed) From the inside to the outside of; out of. [from 14th c.]

quote.citation: c. 1608–1609 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedy of Coriolanus”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene ii]:
quote.text: Can you, when you have pushed out your gates the very defender of them, and in a violent popular ignorance given your enemy your shield, think to front his revenges with the easy groans of old women, the virginal palms of your daughters, or with the palsied intercession of such a decayed dotant as you seem to be?

quote.citation: 1830, Alfred, Lord Tennyson, Adeline:
quote.text: Thy roselips and full blue eyes / Take the heart from out my breast.

quote.citation: 2012, Thomas Gifford, Woman in the Window:
quote.text: After she'd made her single cup of coffee she sat looking out the window into the slushy, halficy backyard and dialed Tony's number on Staten Island.

definitions.definition: A means of exit, escape, reprieve, etc.

(baseball) A state in which a member of the batting team is removed from play due to the application of various rules of the game such as striking out, hitting a fly ball which is caught by the fielding team before bouncing, etc.

quote.citation: 2014, Tom Bentley, Flowering: And Other Stories:
quote.text: The first time I saw Amity we were in front of her house playing work-up, a baseball variation where you move from position to position by outs until you get to bat.

definitions.definition: (cricket) A dismissal; a state in which a member of the batting team finishes his turn at bat, due to the application of various rules of the game, such as the bowler knocking over the batsman's wicket with the ball.
(poker) A card which can make a hand a winner.

quote.citation: 2005, Alison M. Pendergast, Play Winning Poker in No Time, page 57:
quote.text: As a beginner, when you are in a hand, you should practice counting your outs, or those live cards left in the deck that can improve your hand.

quote.citation: 2006, David Apostolico, Lessons from the Professional Poker Tour, page 21:
quote.text: If he did have a bigger ace, I still had at least six outs — the case ace, two nines, and three tens. I could also have more outs if he held anything less than A-K.

definitions.definition: (dated) A trip out; an outing.

quote.citation: 1852 March – 1853 September, Charles Dickens, Bleak House, London: Bradbury and Evans, […], published 1853, →OCLC:
quote.text: Us London lawyers don't often get an out; and when we do, we like to make the most of it, you know.

definitions.definition: (chiefly in the plural) One who, or that which, is out; especially, one who is out of office.

quote.citation: 1827, Benjamin Chew, A Sketch of the Politics, Relations, and Statistics, of the Western World, page 192:
quote.text: This memoir has nothing to do with the question between the ins and the outs; it is intended neither to support nor to assail the administration; it is general in its views upon a general and national subject;  […]

definitions.definition: A place or space outside of something; a nook or corner; an angle projecting outward; an open space.
(printing, dated) A word or words omitted by the compositor in setting up copy; an omission.
(transitive) To eject; to expel.

quote.citation: 1689, John Selden, Table Talk:
quote.text: a king outed of his country

quote.citation: 1674, Peter Heylin, Cosmographie in four bookes:
quote.text: The French have been outed from their holds.

quote.citation: 1925 July – 1926 May, A[rthur] Conan Doyle, “(please specify the chapter number)”, in The Land of Mist (eBook no. 0601351h.html), Australia: Project Gutenberg Australia, published April 2019:
quote.text: "I outed myself for life that night. I can put up a show fight and exhibition bout, but I'm done for the real thing."

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To come or go out; to get out or away; to become public, revealed, or apparent.

quote.citation: c. 1596–1598 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merchant of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene ii]:
quote.text: Truth will out.

quote.citation: 1643, John Milton, Doctrine and Discipline of Divorce:
quote.text: In which Argument he whose courage can serve him to give the first onset, must look for two severall oppositions: the one from those who having sworn themselves to long custom and the letter of the Text, will not out of the road: the other from those whose grosse and vulgar apprehensions conceit but low of matrimoniall purposes, and in the work of male and female think they have all.

quote.citation: 2016 September 28, Tom English, “Celtic 3–3 Manchester City”, in (Please provide the book title or journal name)‎[1], BBC Sport:
quote.text: In those opening minutes City looked like a team that were not ready for Celtic's intensity. They looked a bit shocked to be involved in a fight. Class will out, though.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To reveal (a person or organization) as having a certain secret, such as a being a secret agent or undercover detective.

quote.citation: 2017, Jeph Jacques, Questionable Content (webcomic), Number 3509: Sensitive Information:
quote.text: "Did Dora just offer up that advice, or were you pumping her for information?"  "Shoot, I outed my informant.  I'm a terrible spy."

definitions.definition: (transitive) To reveal (a secret).

quote.citation: 2022 December 16, Alyssa Bailey, “Zendaya Took Tom Holland to Visit Her Old School in Oakland”, in Elle‎[2]:
quote.text: [Tom] Holland himself admitted to GQ last year that the two hadn't really wanted to go public with their dating status. A video of them making out in a car outed their relationship.

definitions.definition: (transitive, LGBTQ) To reveal (a person) as LGBT+ (gay, trans, etc).

quote.citation: 2014 July 18, Jase Peeples, “Susan Blu: Transformation of an Animation Icon”, in The Advocate‎[3]:
quote.text: She throws her head back and lets out a warm laugh before she continues, “After that I thought, What am I so worried about? So I began to tell more people, and the more I outed myself, the easier it got.”

quote.citation: 2015, Juliet Jacques, Trans: A Memoir, Verso Books, →ISBN:
quote.text: Trans Media Watch had recently spoken at the Leveson Inquiry about how the Sun and the Daily Mail routinely outed trans people, publishing old names and photos, for no reason other than because they could.

quote.citation: 2015 December 30, Kathy, “Kathy's Favorite Photo (of Kathy!)”, in Femulate‎[4]:
quote.text: Always in my life I knew I was different. I also accepted that in a way, but I thought I could just live out those desires in private, for myself. I also have gone out en femme for a couple of years.  […]  I outed myself to my sister, which was super positive and is[sic] now my biggest supporter (love u sis!).

quote.citation: 2016, Molly Booth, Saving Hamlet, Little, Brown Books for Young Readers, →ISBN:
quote.text: The Parkses were strict and narrowminded, and not knowing what to do with their recently outed bisexual teenage daughter, their obvious solution was to cut her off from her friends and keep her from leaving the house.

quote.citation: 2020, Jos Twist, Meg-John Barker, Kat Gupta, Benjamin Vincent, Non-Binary Lives: An Anthology of Intersecting Identities, Jessica Kingsley Publishers, →ISBN, page 116:
quote.text: As of 2018, I chair the workforce committee and lead on diversity and inclusion, including heading up a policy review on gender identity and trans inclusion, although that led me to be publicly outed as non-binary in the Sunday Times.

definitions.definition: To kill; to snuff out.

quote.citation: 1912, Arthur Conan Doyle, The Lost World […], London; New York, N.Y.: Hodder and Stoughton, →OCLC:
quote.text: "In my own case, I was beaten about the head by their wings, so we have had a remarkable exhibition of their various methods of offence." "It has been touch and go for our lives," said Lord John, gravely, "and I could not think of a more rotten sort of death than to be outed by such filthy vermin."

definitions.definition: Not at home, or not at one's office or place of employment.
Not in jail, prison, or captivity; freed from confinement.
Not fitted or inserted into something.
(sports) Of the ball or other playing implement, falling or passing or being situated beyond the bounds of the playing area.
Not inside or within a place, especially a place that someone or something was formerly inside or is customarily inside:
(in various games; used especially of a batsman or batter in cricket or baseball) Dismissed from play under the rules of the game.
(of ideas, plans, etc.) Discarded; no longer a possibility.
(of options) No longer acceptable or permissible.
(of certain services, devices, or facilities) Not available; out of service.
(of a user of a service) Not having availability of a service, such as power or communications.
(of lamps, fires etc.) Not shining or burning.
(of an organization, etc.) Temporarily not in operation, or not being attended as usual.

quote.citation: 1990 August 20, PBS NewsHour (TV), DeFrank (actor):
quote.text: No one is out screaming about Congress being out on a month long vacation.

quote.citation: 2012 October 23, Kids As Caregivers Face Special Challenges (radio), via National Public Radio:
quote.text: […]  I had to be there after high school, I mean, after school was out, and after college was out, I had to go straight home.

quote.citation: 2013 August 4, Powerhouse Roundtable (TV), Jeff Zeleny (actor), via ABC:
quote.text: It's a good thing that Congress is out for the month of August  […]

definitions.definition: Unconscious.
No longer popular or in fashion.
Not (or no longer) acceptable or in consideration, play, availability, or operation:
(LGBTQ) Openly acknowledging that one is LGBT+ (gay, trans, etc).

quote.citation: 2011, Allan Bérubé, My Desire for History: Essays in Gay, Community, and Labor History:
quote.text: I had not come out yet and he was out but wasn't; quite ungay, I would say, and yet gay.

quote.citation: 2018, Matthew Waites, Supporting Young Transgender Men: A Guide for Professionals, Jessica Kingsley Publishers, →ISBN, page 40:
quote.text: However, for a transgender man, while living stealth can be a feasible option for some, key people will need to know  […]  Not everyone has to be out, loud  and proud or march down the streets holding trans flags  […]

definitions.definition: (by extension, uncommon) Open, public; public about or openly acknowledging some (usually specified)  identity.

quote.citation: 2014, Arlene Stein, Reluctant Witnesses: Survivors, Their Children, and the Rise of Holocaust Consciousness, Oxford University Press, →ISBN:
quote.text: She was “out” as a survivor for the first time in her life. “I had friends who had known me many, many years who are totally astounded, shocked,” she said. “They could not believe that I was a Holocaust survivor.  […] ”

definitions.definition: Open or public (about something).
Freed from secrecy.
Released, available for purchase, download or other use.

quote.citation: 2009, Roger Stahl, Militainment, Inc.: War, Media, and Popular Culture, page 96:
quote.text: The game was commercially released on Xbox and PC in 2005 as an installment of the Close Combat series, which had been out since 1996.

definitions.definition: (of flowers) In bloom.
(of the sun, moon or stars) Visible in the sky; not obscured by clouds.
(obsolete) Of a young lady: having entered society and available to be courted.

quote.citation: 1814 May 9, [Jane Austen], chapter V, in Mansfield Park: […], volume I, London:  […]  [George Sidney] for T[homas] Egerton, […], →OCLC, page 98:
quote.text: "Pray, is she out, or is she not?—I am puzzled.—She dined at the Parsonage, with the rest of you, which seemed like being out; and yet she says so little, that I can hardly suppose she is."

definitions.definition: Available to be seen, or to be interacted with in some way:
Of the tide, at or near its lowest level.
Without; no longer in possession of; not having any more.
(of calculations or measurements) Containing errors or discrepancies, or in error by a stated amount.
(procedure word, especially military) A radio procedure word meaning that the station is finished with its transmission and does not expect a response.

quote.citation: 2002 November 18, Nintendo R&D1, Metroid Fusion, Nintendo, Game Boy Advance, scene: dispatch:
quote.text: [Galactic Federation official]: 'Does Samus suspect anything?' / Ship AI: 'No, I do not think so.' / [Galactic Federation official]: 'Good. Monitor her closely.' / Ship AI: 'Affirmative. Out.'

definitions.definition: Get out; begone; away!

quote.citation: c. 1606 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Macbeth”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, (please specify the act number in uppercase Roman numerals, and the scene number in lowercase Roman numerals):
quote.text: Out, damned spot! Out, I say!
